name: Nazism
info: Nazism, formally National Socialism, was the far-right, ultranationalist and racist ideology of Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party, which arose in Germany after 1919, built a one-party dictatorship and carried out the Holocaust.

facts.thinkers: Adolf Hitler, whose personal views the movement treated as final on ideology; Joseph Goebbels, propagandist and anti-capitalist radical; Alfred Rosenberg, who introduced Hitler to the Protocols of the Elders of Zion; Hans F. K. Günther, racial theorist; Carl Schmitt, legal theorist of the Führerprinzip; Heinrich Himmler, head of the SS; Gregor and Otto Strasser, anti-capitalist rivals; earlier influences Fichte, Gobineau, Houston Stewart Chamberlain, Madison Grant, Johann Plenge and Oswald Spengler
facts.texts: Hitler’s Mein Kampf and Zweites Buch; the party programme of 1920 (the 25-point plan); Goebbels’s Der Nazi-Sozi; Günther’s Rassenkunde des deutschen Volkes (1922); Schmitt’s Staat, Bewegung, Volk (1933); among its sources Chamberlain’s The Foundations of the Nineteenth Century (1899), Grant’s The Passing of the Great Race (1916) and Spengler’s The Decline of the West (1918)
facts.ideas: a racial hierarchy with a supposed Aryan master race; fervent antisemitism; Lebensraum, or living space, through conquest in the East; the Führerprinzip, absolute obedience to a single leader; the Volksgemeinschaft, a racial people’s community without class conflict; anti-communism and rejection of liberal democracy; social Darwinism and eugenics; a totalitarian state
facts.today: Nazism became widely regarded as evil after 1945. Only a few fringe racist groups, usually called neo-Nazis, describe themselves as its followers, and the use of Nazi symbols is illegal in many European countries.

t: Nazism combined German ultranationalism, antisemitism and pseudo-scientific racial theory with the Führerprinzip and the aim of winning Lebensraum in Eastern Europe, and it took much of its material from movements that existed in Germany before 1914.

Hitler was appointed Chancellor in January 1933 by President Hindenburg with the support of conservative nationalists who believed they could control him; the Nazis then used the Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act to build a one-party state.

Under Nazi rule Jews, Romani, political opponents and other people deemed undesirable were marginalised, imprisoned or murdered, and in the Holocaust millions, including two-thirds of Europe’s Jewish population, were exterminated.
dyk: The word nazi was a colloquial, derogatory word for a backward farmer before the party existed; the party’s labour-movement opponents shortened its name to it in the 1920s, and the Nazis themselves first used it in 1926, in Joseph Goebbels’s Der Nazi-Sozi.
ev: The German Workers’ Party, the Nazi Party’s precursor, is founded
The party is renamed the National Socialist German Workers’ Party to appeal to left-wing workers, a change Hitler at first opposed
The Nazis’ attempted “March on Berlin”, modelled on Mussolini’s March on Rome, ends in the failed Beer Hall Putsch in Munich
The Nazi Party becomes the largest party in the German parliament without a majority
Hitler is appointed Chancellor in January; the Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act follow, and the Nazis establish a one-party state
Hitler purges Ernst Röhm and other SA leaders in the Night of the Long Knives
The Nuremberg Laws ban sexual relations and marriage between Germans and Jews
Nazi Germany collapses, and the full extent of the Holocaust is disclosed

sections.origins:
Historians trace the roots of Nazism to elements of European political culture in circulation before 1914, which Joachim Fest called a “scrapheap of ideas”. Martin Broszat held that almost all its essential elements were present in the radical protest movements of pre-1914 Germany: a virulent antisemitism, a blood-and-soil ideology, the notion of a master race and the idea of territorial acquisition and settlement in the East. Its ultranationalism came from pan-Germanism and the ethno-nationalist Völkisch movement, and the Freikorps paramilitary groups formed after Germany’s defeat in the First World War were the origin of the party’s “cult of violence”.

Thinkers who influenced it included Johann Gottlieb Fichte, whose Speeches to the German Nation (1808) called for a German national revolution against the French occupiers, and the racial theorists Arthur de Gobineau, Houston Stewart Chamberlain and Madison Grant; Hitler called Grant’s The Passing of the Great Race (1916) “my Bible”. In Vienna Hitler was influenced by Georg Ritter von Schönerer, from whom he took the Heil greeting and the Führer title, and impressed by the antisemitic populism of Karl Lueger.

The sociologist Johann Plenge spoke during the First World War of a “National Socialism” within the “ideas of 1914”, and Oswald Spengler’s writings influenced the Nazis. Benito Mussolini’s March on Rome in 1922 won Hitler’s admiration, and the Nazis’ “March on Berlin” of 1923, modelled on it, ended in the failed Beer Hall Putsch in Munich.
sections.ideas:
Nazism held a bio-geo-political worldview that sought territorial expansion to cultivate what it called a “purified and homogeneous Aryan population”. It emphasised pseudo-scientific theories of racial hierarchy in which ethnic Germans and Nordic-Aryans were a master race. It claimed that Jews were a mixed race responsible for the exploitation of the Aryans, and it classed Slavs as Untermenschen, “subhumans”. Hitler declared a racial conflict against the Jews to be necessary, and Nazi writers such as Hans F. K. Günther supplied the racial classifications.

Nazi doctrine held that life was an eternal struggle and that natural selection favoured the strong, so that protecting those it declared inferior was said to prevent nature from taking its course. Its Lebensraum doctrine claimed that Germany needed land in the East, above all in Russia, and Hitler’s Mein Kampf proposed an alliance with Britain and Italy against the Soviet Union. The Führerprinzip placed a single leader at the head of a hierarchy in which each member owed absolute obedience to those above him.

Nazism rejected Marxist class conflict and egalitarianism in favour of the Volksgemeinschaft, a racial “people’s community” that kept private property and social classes but subordinated them to the nation. It opposed liberal democracy and aimed at a totalitarian state; Hitler declared that “there are no longer any free realms in which the individual belongs to himself”. Broszat judged that its ideology was vague and gained reality only through Hitler.
sections.spread:
Nazism arose in Germany. The German Workers’ Party was founded in 1919 and renamed the National Socialist German Workers’ Party in 1920. The Nazis’ voters were mainly farmers and the middle class, and after 1929 wealthy donors and industrialists, who saw the party as a bulwark against communism, began to fund it. In 1931 the Nazis joined monarchists, the German National People’s Party and others in the Harzburg Front against the Weimar Republic, an alliance the Nazis called tactical.

The party had factions. Conservative Nazis such as Hermann Göring urged conciliation with capitalists, while radicals such as Joseph Goebbels and the Strasser brothers stressed anti-capitalism; the Strassers left in 1930 to found the Black Front. The SA under Ernst Röhm pressed for a “second revolution”. The Nazi Party became the largest party in the Reichstag in the elections of 1932, and Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933.

Hitler modelled the party on Italian Fascism, presented the Nazis as a form of German fascism, and Mussolini eventually spoke of “German Fascism”. Anti-communist regimes and groups that supported Nazism in the 1930s and 1940s included the Falange in Francoist Spain, the Vichy regime in France and the British Union of Fascists under Oswald Mosley. After 1945 small neo-Nazi parties appeared in several European countries; the Socialist Reich Party, founded in West Germany in 1949, was banned by the Federal Constitutional Court in 1952.
sections.power:
Hitler was appointed Chancellor in January 1933 by President Paul von Hindenburg, with the support of conservative nationalists who believed they could control him. Using the Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act, the Nazis established a one-party state and began Gleichschaltung, or Nazification. The Communist Party was banned; 4,000 of its officials were arrested in February 1933, and by the end of the year 130,000 communists had been sent to concentration camps. In 1934 Hitler purged Röhm and other SA leaders in the Night of the Long Knives.

The regime applied “racial hygiene”. A law of 1933 prescribed compulsory sterilisation for people with conditions thought hereditary, and an estimated 360,000 people were sterilised between 1933 and 1939; the euthanasia of disabled people was later named Action T4. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 banned sexual relations and marriage between Germans and Jews and were later extended to Romani and Black people. Between 1937 and 1939 the regime arrested 95,000 homosexual men, and those sent to camps wore pink triangles.

Jews, Romani, political opponents and other “undesirable” people were marginalised, imprisoned or murdered. During the Second World War millions, including two-thirds of Europe’s Jewish population, were exterminated in the genocide known as the Holocaust. Hitler’s ambition at the start of the war was to exterminate, expel or enslave Slavs from Central and Eastern Europe. At home, public works and rearmament cut unemployment by 40 per cent in one year, and military spending rose from 1 to 10 per cent of national income in the regime’s first two years.
sections.critiques:
Some of the movement’s early supporters turned against it. Kaiser Wilhelm II, who had at first supported the Nazis, called them a “bunch of shirted gangsters” and, after Kristallnacht in 1938, said he was ashamed to be a German. Otto von Habsburg rejected Nazism for Austria and was sentenced to death by the Nazis after the annexation. Oswald Spengler, an influence on the movement, opposed its antisemitism, writing that one who would rather destroy business and scholarship than see Jews in them “is an ideologue, i.e., a danger for the nation”. The Catholic Church opposed Nazi sterilisation laws and forbade its members to vote for the Nazis until the concordat of July 1933.

Scholars dispute how to classify it. The majority identify Nazism as far-right, while Hitler and others at times called it a party of the right and at times denied that it was left or right. It has been called reactionary, though it looked back to a mythic Germany rather than to the pre-Weimar monarchy, and it has been seen as the result of a crisis of capitalism, a “totalitarian monopoly capitalism”. Richard Overy describes the Nazi war economy as a mixed economy between the command economy of the USSR and the capitalist system of the US. Michael Burleigh calls its spirituality “self-consciously pagan and primitive”, while Roger Griffin rejects the claim that it was primarily pagan, noting that neo-pagans such as Himmler and Rosenberg were a minority.

Hannah Arendt held that Nazism appealed as a totalitarian ideology because it offered clear solutions after the First World War and the Depression. Adam Tooze rejects the view that the regime faced a choice of “guns or butter”, and argues that its interest in agrarian life reflected a society still in economic transition.
sections.legacy:
After Germany’s defeat and the public disclosure of the full extent of the Holocaust, Nazism became widely regarded as evil. Overt expressions of support for Nazi ideas were prohibited in Germany and other European countries, and the use of Nazi symbols is illegal in many of them. Only a few fringe racist groups, usually called neo-Nazis, describe themselves as its followers; many espouse white supremacy and deliberately adopt the symbols of Nazi Germany.

A report to the United Nations Human Rights Council in 2018 noted that neo-Nazi groups use online platforms and popular culture to spread their ideology, including in countries where Nazism is banned. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres has described neo-Nazis and white supremacists as increasingly organised and able to recruit across borders. Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution has named neo-Nazism in its annual reports as a persistent internal security threat.

Historians regard the equation of Nazism with “Hitlerism” as too simplistic, since the ideologies it took in were established in parts of German society long before the First World War. Broszat held that it was a charismatic movement whose ideology was incorporated in Hitler; because the ideology came from Hitler’s personal views, the party programme, the aims of the Völkisch and nationalist movements and conflicts between party functionaries, its analysis is usually descriptive.

summary: Nazism, formally National Socialism, was the racist, antisemitic and totalitarian ideology of Hitler and the Nazi Party, built on claims of an Aryan master race and the pursuit of Lebensraum. In power from 1933, it created a one-party state and carried out the Holocaust, in which two-thirds of Europe’s Jews were exterminated.

Richard J. Evans, The Coming of the Third Reich (Penguin Books, 2003)
Richard J. Evans, The Third Reich in Power (Penguin Books, 2005)
Adam Tooze, The Wages of Destruction: The Making and Breaking of the Nazi Economy (Viking, 2006)
notes: end 1945: the article dates Nazism's ending only as the collapse of Nazi Germany in 1945; neo-Nazi groups after the war are treated as a separate fringe, so end is not null.
start 1919 is the founding of the German Workers' Party; the article places the roots before 1914 and gives no single founding text with a year (Mein Kampf has no year in the article).
No total death toll for the Holocaust beyond 'millions, including two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population'; the article gives no figures for Roma, Slavs or the war.
The article's 'Classification: reactionary or revolutionary?' section is cut off mid-sentence; I used only its complete sentences.

Left out: the article's Russian officials' claims (Putin, Lavrov) about a Nazi revival, as present politics; the section on use of the American racist model; the sex and gender, religion and economics details beyond those used; the Spartan euthanasia justification.
The article's sentence on the SA/Röhm 'first revolution' and Hitler's 1934 purge appears in three places; used once.
Gobineau, Chamberlain and Grant are listed as influences, as the article states; the article says the Nazis rejected Hegel and condemned Haeckel, not used.
